title: Glasses and opening
subtitle: The tools that help
objectives: Choose a glass that helps a wine show well
Open still and sparkling wines safely

steps.title: The right glass
steps.body: A good glass has a bowl that narrows at the top, to gather aromas, and a stem so your hand doesn't warm the wine. Fill to about a third so you can swirl. Larger bowls suit aromatic reds; narrower ones keep whites cool. A tall flute keeps bubbles but hides aroma, so many prefer a white wine glass for Champagne.
steps.highlight: Bowl that narrows, a stem, a third full

steps.title: Why a sparkling cork flies
steps.body: A bottle of Champagne holds about 6 atmospheres of pressure. If the cork is released fast, it can leave at over 40 km/h. Keep a thumb on the cork, point it away from people, and twist the bottle, not the cork, letting the gas out with a sigh rather than a pop.
steps.highlight: Twist the bottle, not the cork

steps.prompt: Put the steps for opening a sparkling wine in order.
items: Loosen the wire cage, thumb on the cork
Tilt the bottle away from people
Let the cork ease out with a sigh
steps.explanation: Keeping the thumb on the cork from the moment the cage loosens is the key safety step.

steps.title: Decanting
steps.body: Pouring a wine into a decanter does two jobs. It separates an old red or vintage Port from its sediment, the solids that form with age. And it gives a young, tight wine air, which can open up its aromas. Pour slowly in front of a light and stop when you see sediment reach the neck.
steps.highlight: Decant for sediment or for air

steps.prompt: Decanting is only useful for very old wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Old wines are decanted for sediment, but young, tannic reds are often decanted for air, which helps their aromas open.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A bowl that narrows, a stem and a third full help any wine
Open sparkling wine by holding the cork and twisting the bottle
Decant old wines for sediment and young ones for air
